newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian police launch hunt for missing girl.
newsitem.headline: Belgian police launch hunt for missing girl.

text.p: Belgian police said on Thursday they had launched a full-scale search for a 17-year-old girl who has been missing for nearly a month and whose adoptive parents are convinced she is not a runaway.
"The case has been put under investigation," a spokesman said.

The slow response of police to the family's appeals for help after Lamya Zouboudi disappeared while out shopping on June 28 has prompted comparisons in the Belgian media with the failings of the hunt for eight-year-old Loubna Benaissa.
Loubna, who went missing in 1992, was found dead in March this year, stuffed into a steel trunk in the basement of a Brussels garage.
Police had taken days to start investigations despite the family's pleas, and had searched the garage where her body was eventually found.
Loubna's body was the fifth to be found in seven months in a paedophile scandal that is still rocking Belgium and has triggered wide-ranging reforms of the police and justice system.

Convicted child rapist Marc Dutroux has been charged with the murder of four of the girls, and convicted child molester Patrick Derochette has been charged with illegal imprisonment and rape leading to the death of a child under 10 years of age.
Police are still searching for at least seven other children who have disappeared without trace over the years.
An all-party parliamentary committee investigating the original police investigations issued a report in April listing bungling and failures by police and magistrates.
Belgian ecological parties, a small minority in the parliament, on Wednesday called on the government to resign over what they said was its slow response to the scandals.

The formal motion, which will be tabled when parliament returns from recess in September, has no chance of success but will nevertheless serve as a focal point for popular discontent with the political establishment.

Last October more than a quarter of a million people marched through Brussels in an unprecedented demonstration of disgust with a system widely seen as having failed the people and served only itself.

Many so-called white march committees are still active and regularly hold small demonstrations -- the most recent having been during Belgian national day on Monday when King Albert repeated his Christmas call for a fundamental change in society.

The all-party parliamentary committee is still investigating its theories that Dutroux and his accomplices -- including his second wife -- may have been able to escape detection for so long because they had high-level protection.
The report is due at the end of September.
